drills.q: Explain exactly how a Cloud Logging exclusion filter saves money, and what happens if the excluded log is also exported via a sink.
drills.a: The Log Router evaluates exclusion filters before ingestion -- a match means the entry is never billed at Logging's $0.50/GiB rate. If a sink independently exports that same log to Pub/Sub, GCS, or BigQuery, the export still happens; you pay that destination's normal (usually far cheaper) rate instead. Net effect: retain a log for compliance at a fraction of the cost by routing it around Logging bucket storage entirely -- but you lose Logging's native structured querying/alerting on that excluded data, which is the real tradeoff.

drills.q: Distinguish the four Cloud Audit Log types and state which are free and which are chargeable, with the biggest cost-risk one flagged.
drills.a: Admin Activity (config/metadata-modifying API calls) -- free, always on, cannot be disabled. System Event (Google-initiated actions on your resources) -- free, part of the same _Required bucket. Data Access (reads/writes on data itself, e.g. BigQuery queries, GCS object reads) -- chargeable, off by default except a few services; this is the most common source of an unexpected audit-logging cost spike on query-heavy workloads. Policy Denied (blocked access attempts) -- chargeable for storage, on by default.

drills.q: Design a tiered burn-rate alerting policy for a service with a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days, and explain why a single static threshold underperforms it.
drills.a: Fast-burn tier (e.g. 10x rate over a 1-hour lookback, budget exhausted in ~3 days if sustained) pages on-call immediately. Slow-burn tier (e.g. 2x rate over a longer lookback like 6 hours) opens a ticket, catching gradual degradation the 1-hour window would miss since the hourly rate looks unremarkable even while steadily draining the month's budget. A static error-rate threshold has no concept of remaining budget -- it fires identically whether 95% or 5% of budget remains, producing both false urgency on budget-cheap noise and missed slow burns.

drills.q: A team's Cloud Trace shows suspiciously few error traces despite a known elevated error rate in the logs. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Likely head-based sampling at a low fixed rate (5-10%) where the sample/drop decision is made before the request's outcome is known -- this randomly drops most requests including a proportional share of actual errors, giving a representative sample of all traffic but not of the interesting (error) traffic. Fix: add tail-based sampling via an OpenTelemetry Collector, deferring the keep/drop decision until the full trace including outcome is known, so errors and slow outliers are retained at a much higher rate than routine successful requests.

drills.q: Explain the difference between Sustained Use Discounts and Committed Use Discounts on GCP, and why AWS has no direct equivalent to the former.
drills.a: SUDs: automatic, zero commitment, up to 30% off once a qualifying VM (N1/N2/N2D/C2/M1/M2 only) runs more than 25% of the billing month -- no purchase action required. CUDs: explicit commitment to vCPU+memory for 1yr (37%) or 3yr (55%), no-upfront-only. AWS's Reserved Instances and Savings Plans both require an explicit commitment -- there's no AWS mechanism granting an automatic discount purely from sustained usage with zero commitment, a genuine structural difference.

drills.q: Why did GCP move the default Committed Use Discount scope from project to billing account in 2026, and what specific problem did it fix?
drills.a: Under project-scoped CUDs, a commitment sized against one project's usage could become stranded (underutilized, still paid for) if that project's workload shrank, even while another project in the same org had growing usage that could have absorbed the committed capacity. Billing-account scoping lets one commitment apply automatically across any eligible usage in the account, fixing the classic 'committed based on Project A, then Project A shrank' failure -- though it doesn't protect against the org's total eligible usage shrinking, which still requires conservative sizing.

drills.q: A candidate says SLOs and raw uptime percentages are basically the same thing. Correct this precisely.
drills.a: An uptime percentage alone is just a number; an SLO formalizes it against a specific measurable SLI (e.g. fraction of requests under a latency threshold, or non-5xx rate), a compliance period (e.g. rolling 30 days), and an error budget derived from the gap to 100% -- which is what enables burn-rate alerting and release-gating. Two services both reporting '99.9% uptime' can have very different SLO definitions (different SLIs, different windows, different traffic volumes producing very different absolute tolerable-failure counts) that aren't directly comparable without knowing those specifics.

drills.q: Design a FinOps commitment strategy for a workload on N2 instances with genuinely unpredictable, growing usage. Should you buy CUDs, and how much?
drills.a: The automatic Sustained Use Discount (up to 30%, zero commitment, applies to N2) already captures meaningful savings with zero stranding risk. Any CUD purchase should be sized conservatively below the historical MINIMUM observed usage, not average or the Recommender's raw suggestion, so even if growth stalls the committed portion stays fully utilized. Usage above that conservative floor rides on SUDs/no-discount until the growth trajectory is established enough to justify committing further -- buying to current peak/average on a volatile workload risks paying for underutilized committed capacity the moment growth slows.

drills.q: Explain why enabling verbose Data Access audit logs on a high-QPS BigQuery workload without mitigation is a common, expensive mistake, and what the correct mitigation is (not disabling it).
drills.a: Data Access logs capture every query execution on BigQuery specifically -- a high-QPS analytics workload can generate audit-log volume comparable to or exceeding actual query traffic, and since Data Access logs are chargeable at the standard $0.50/GiB rate with no discount, this can become one of the largest Logging line items. Correct mitigation: scope Data Access logging precisely (only datasets genuinely needing the audit trail) and export to a cheap destination (BigQuery/GCS) via a sink rather than leaving it in the chargeable _Default bucket -- not disabling it wholesale, since compliance/security requirements often make it a hard requirement.

drills.q: Compare Cloud Logging's and CloudWatch Logs' free tiers and per-GB pricing, and state the practical implication for a migration.
drills.a: Both charge roughly $0.50/GB ingestion, but Cloud Logging's free tier is 50 GiB/month versus CloudWatch Logs' 5 GB/month -- a 10x difference. A team migrating a logging-heavy workload from AWS gets meaningfully more runway before costs become material on GCP purely from the larger free tier. At real production volume well beyond either free tier, the rates converge and the deciding cost factor becomes operational hygiene (exclusion filters, targeted sinks, retention tuning) on either platform, not the free-tier size.

drills.q: A service's SLO burn-rate alert correctly fires, but the root cause is a dependency's outage entirely outside the team's control. Was the alerting wrong, and should the dependency's failures be excluded from the SLI going forward?
drills.a: The alerting was not wrong -- burn-rate alerts are deliberately cause-agnostic, measuring user-observed budget consumption regardless of root cause; a downstream dependency degrading this service's SLI is still real user impact and correctly surfaced. The default answer to excluding it is no: doing so risks the SLO no longer reflecting actual user experience, defeating its purpose. If the dependency's failures are common enough to meaningfully distort the SLO, the better fix is improving resilience (retries, fallbacks, circuit breakers) or renegotiating the SLO target with that dependency's reliability factored in -- not quietly excluding inconvenient data from the measurement.

drills.q: Why is Cloud Trace's sampling strategy decision rarely driven by its direct billing cost, and what actually drives it?
drills.a: At 2.5M free spans/month and $0.20/million beyond, Cloud Trace's direct cost is negligible relative to compute or Logging spend for most workloads -- optimizing sampling purely to minimize that line item targets the wrong number. The real drivers are downstream trace storage/query cost and latency at high retained volume, signal-to-noise for engineers investigating incidents (too much routine data buries the interesting traces), and the need to preferentially retain error/slow-outlier traces over routine successful ones -- which is a signal-quality problem tail-based sampling addresses directly and head-based sampling only addresses probabilistically.
